common_name: Angelus Bearded Iris (Historic 1937 Egelberg Light Pink Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Angelus is a historic light pink tall bearded iris best remembered as a parent of the 1948 introduction 'Pathfinder'.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun in loose, well-drained soil. Angelus was bred by Leo Egelberg from a cross of 'Elizabeth Egelberg' and 'Depute Nomblot' and introduced in 1937, producing fresh light pink standards over pink falls with a faint lavender iridescence beneath a bright lemon-yellow beard. It earned an Honorable Mention in 1938 and an Award of Merit in 1939, and its chief legacy today is as one of the two parents, crossed with 'Mirabelle', behind Mrs. C. Whiting's 1948 iris 'Pathfinder'. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom, keeping rhizomes shallow and in full sun.

common_name: Trosuperba Bearded Iris (Historic 1912 Farr Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Trosuperba is an early-20th-century tall bearded iris remembered chiefly for its role as breeding stock behind later red and purple-toned introductions.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed to sunlight in loose, well-drained soil in full sun. Trosuperba was bred by American hybridizer Bertrand H. Farr and introduced in 1912, a tall bearded form derived from Iris trojana breeding stock that was widely used in the following decades to push deeper color saturation into early American iris lines. Its own flower is less documented today than its breeding legacy: English hybridizer Arthur J. Bliss crossed it with his blue-purple bitone 'Dominion' to produce 'Cardinal' in 1919, carrying Trosuperba's influence into the trans-Atlantic iris breeding programs of the following generation. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom, discarding old woody rhizomes.

common_name: Hector Bearded Iris (Historic Parent Cultivar Behind Rose Madder)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Hector is a historic tall bearded iris documented today chiefly through its role as a breeding parent.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed to the sun in loose, well-drained soil in full sun. Hector is a historic tall bearded iris remembered today almost entirely through its role as a breeding parent: crossed with 'Shelford Chieftain' and then selfed, it produced pioneering American hybridizer Grace Sturtevant's 1920 introduction 'Rose Madder', which went on to become the pollen parent of the 1929 Dykes Medal winner 'Dauntless'. No reliable record of Hector's own flower color, hybridizer, or introduction date survives in the sources consulted, a common gap for early-20th-century parent cultivars overshadowed by their more famous descendants. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom, keeping rhizomes shallow and in full sun.

common_name: Shelford Chieftain Bearded Iris (Historic 1909 Foster Blue Bitone Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Shelford Chieftain is a foundational early-20th-century tall bearded iris bred by Sir Michael Foster.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed to sunlight in well-drained soil in full sun. Shelford Chieftain was raised by British physiologist and amateur iris breeder Sir Michael Foster and introduced in 1909 as a sibling seedling to his 'Lady Foster', carrying medium blue, midseason bitone flowers descended from his pioneering crosses of Iris cypriana and Iris trojana toward the Iris pallida lines that underpin most modern tall bearded iris. Rather than winning awards in its own era, its lasting significance is as foundational breeding stock: crossed with 'Hector' and then selfed, it produced Grace Sturtevant's 1920 'Rose Madder', ancestor of the 1929 Dykes Medal winner 'Dauntless'. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom, discarding the oldest central rhizomes.

common_name: Fragrant Sapphire Bearded Iris (Historic 1959 Schortman Blue Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Fragrant Sapphire is a tall, late-blooming blue bearded iris bred by William Schortman.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil in full sun. Fragrant Sapphire was bred by William Schortman from his own seedling line and registered in 1959, producing blue tall bearded flowers on a sturdy 40-inch stalk blooming midseason to late. Sanford Babson crossed it with his seedling K97 to produce 'Epic', registered at his Melrose Gardens in the mid-1960s and later used to breed the 1974 Dykes Medal winner 'Shipshape'. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to keep plantings vigorous.

common_name: Mirabelle Bearded Iris (Historic 1941 Whiting Apricot-Pink Blend Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; this Mirabelle is a tall bearded iris bred by Mrs. C. Whiting, unrelated to the French Mirabelle plum of the same name.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil in full sun; this Mirabelle is a tall bearded iris, unrelated to the French Mirabelle plum of the same name. Bred by Mrs. C. (Agnes) Whiting from a cross of 'Matula' and 'Happy Days', it was registered in 1940 and introduced in 1941, bearing a creamy apricot-to-orient-pink blend over a deep orange beard on a 38-inch stalk, and earned an Honorable Mention that year. Whiting later crossed it with 'Angelus' to breed her own 1948 introduction 'Pathfinder', which in turn became a grandparent of the 1963 Dykes Medal winner 'Amethyst Flame'. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom, replanting only vigorous outer rhizomes.

common_name: Witches' Sabbath Bearded Iris (Historic 1986 Maryott Purple-Black Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Witches' Sabbath is a ruffled purple-black tall bearded iris bred by William Maryott.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed to sunlight in well-drained soil in full sun. Witches' Sabbath was bred by William Maryott from a cross of 'Waltzing Widow' and a seedling descended from 'Prophecy' and 'Gypsy Belle' crossed with 'Intuition', registered in 1982 and introduced in 1986, producing heavily ruffled purple-black standards over velvety purple-black falls set off by old-gold beards on a 36 to 38-inch stalk. It earned an Honorable Mention in 1988, and Paul Black later crossed it with Barry Blyth's 'In Town' to breed and name 'Tom Johnson' after his Mid-America Iris Garden business partner. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to keep plantings vigorous.

common_name: In Town Bearded Iris (Historic 1988 Blyth Blue-Lavender Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; In Town is an early-blooming blue-lavender tall bearded iris bred by Australian hybridizer Barry Blyth.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil in full sun. In Town was bred by Australian hybridizer Barry Blyth from a cross of 'Tomorrow's Child' and 'Magic Man', registered in 1985 and introduced in 1988, producing blue-lavender standards over velvety blue-purple falls edged in lavender, with a tangerine-red beard tipped lavender, blooming early to midseason on a 38-inch stalk. It earned an Honorable Mention and a Favorite Guest award in 1990, and was later crossed with William Maryott's 'Witches' Sabbath' by Paul Black to breed 'Tom Johnson'. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom, discarding old woody rhizomes.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; the Apothecary's Rose is one of the oldest documented garden roses, cultivated for medicinal and perfume use since at least the 1200s.

directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; this ancient Gallica tolerates lean soil and benign neglect far better than modern roses. Grown for drying and apothecary use since at least the thirteenth century at Provins, France, where Thibaud IV of Champagne made it a civic emblem, it later became known in England as the red rose badge of the House of Lancaster during the Wars of the Roses. Its semi-double, deep pink-to-crimson flowers are intensely fragrant and, unusually, grow more strongly scented as the petals dry rather than losing fragrance, the trait that made them prized for rosewater, conserves, and medicinal sachets for centuries. Like other Gallicas it blooms once in a heavy, fragrant spring flush on a dense, well-branched, disease-resistant shrub, and is the un-striped parent of the famous sport 'Rosa Mundi'.

common_name: Mitchellena American Persimmon (Historic Indiana Breeding-Line Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant a grafted bare-root or container tree in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Mitchellena is documented chiefly as a breeding-line parent behind the modern selection 'Valeene Beauty'.

directions: Plant a grafted bare-root or container tree in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; like other named American persimmon selections it sets fruit without needing a separate pollinator. Mitchellena, also recorded under the synonyms 'Lena' and 'Mitchell', is an Indiana-origin selection held in collections such as the Dawes Arboretum, documented today chiefly as the seed parent James Claypool crossed with 'Early Golden' to breed his heavy-bearing selection Claypool I-94, later named 'Valeene Beauty'. Independently verified detail on Mitchellena's own fruit size, ripening season, or flavor beyond this breeding role is thin in the sources consulted, a common gap for older regional persimmon parent selections. As with all Diospyros virginiana cultivars, fruit remains astringent and unpalatable until it softens fully after frost, after which it turns rich and sweet.

common_name: Lady Kesteven Daffodil (Historic 1921 Backhouse Pink-Cupped Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Lady Kesteven is a Division 3 small-cupped daffodil bred by pioneering pink-daffodil hybridizer Sarah Backhouse.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in fall. Lady Kesteven was bred by Sarah Backhouse, one of the earliest hybridizers to pursue pink-cupped daffodils, and registered in 1921 as a Division 3 small-cupped cultivar with a white perianth surrounding a cup tinged orange. It was later used as the pollen parent, crossed with 'Pink Rim', by Dutch hybridizer P.B. van Eeden to breed his 1970 introduction 'Pink Pride', one of the first daffodils with a crown distinctly tinged pink. Let the foliage die back naturally after bloom to recharge the bulb for the following spring.

common_name: Pink Rim Daffodil (Historic 1939 Dutch Large-Cupped Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Pink Rim is a Division 2 large-cupped daffodil registered in 1939 by the Dutch firm L. van Leeuwen & Son.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in fall. Pink Rim was registered in 1939 by the Dutch firm L. van Leeuwen & Son as a Division 2 large-cupped daffodil, with a white perianth around a corona that opens yellow and matures to white with a broad, sunproof pink band at the flared, ribbed, and finely crenate rim. Dutch hybridizer P.B. van Eeden later used it as the seed parent, crossed with 'Lady Kesteven', to breed his 1970 introduction 'Pink Pride'. It increases into large clumps over the years; deadhead spent blooms if desired but allow the foliage to die back fully before removing it.

common_name: Bagatelle Daffodil (Historic 1965 Dutch Miniature Yellow Trumpet Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun in fall; Bagatelle is a Division 1 miniature trumpet daffodil registered in 1965 by the Dutch firm J. Gerritsen and Son.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Bagatelle was registered in 1965 by the Dutch firm J. Gerritsen and Son as a Division 1 miniature trumpet daffodil, bearing a solid yellow perianth and trumpet on a diminutive scale comparable to its better-known relative 'Wee Bee'. It has since been used as breeding stock for further miniature introductions, including crosses with Narcissus cyclamineus that produced later novelty miniatures. Grow it in a rock garden, trough, or raised bed where its small scale will not be lost among larger bulbs, and let the foliage die back fully after bloom.

common_name: Capron Royal Musk Strawberry (Historic French Hautbois Strawberry)

planting.note: Plant runners or divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Capron Royal is a historic French-origin musk strawberry strain, not an Italian one despite some secondary sources' mislabeling.

directions: Plant runners or divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun. Capron Royal descends from 'Le Chapiron', a musk strawberry strain grown in France from the 1570s and later cultivated in the royal kitchen garden at Versailles for Louis XIV, with a hermaphroditic, self-fruitful strain of the name documented in Russian seed and plant catalogs by the 1860s. Like other musk strawberries it bears small, intensely perfumed fruit with a complex scent often compared to a blend of strawberry, pineapple, and rose, far more aromatic than modern garden strawberries. Because most musk strawberry stock is single-sexed, plant it alongside a known male clone to ensure reliable fruit set.
sources: historical Potager du Roi, Versailles records

planting.note: Move potted canes outdoors to a bright, sheltered, partly shaded spot once nights stay above 50F; Kentwood is a tall, upright cane-type begonia best known as a parent of 'Irene Nuss'.

directions: Plant in bright, filtered light in a rich, fast-draining potting mix; Kentwood is a tall, upright cane-type (angel-wing) begonia with large, gracefully lobed, silver-spotted leaves on sturdy canes that need little staking. Clusters of fragrant, pendulous pink flowers appear from late summer into fall, held well above the foliage. It was crossed with 'Lenore Olivier' to breed the widely grown 1971 California introduction 'Irene Nuss'. Pinch young canes to encourage branching, let the topsoil dry slightly between waterings, and feed lightly through the growing season.

common_name: Lenore Olivier Begonia (Dark Pink-Flowered Cane Begonia)

planting.note: Move potted canes outdoors to a bright, sheltered, partly shaded spot once nights stay above 50F; Lenore Olivier is a sturdy upright cane-type begonia best known as a parent of 'Irene Nuss'.

directions: Plant in bright, filtered light in a rich, fast-draining potting mix; Lenore Olivier is a sturdy, upright cane-type begonia with large, dark green leaves on canes substantial enough to need little staking even as the plant matures. Medium-to-large, dark pink flowers appear in hanging clusters through summer and fall. It was crossed with 'Kentwood' to breed the popular 1971 introduction 'Irene Nuss', and has also been used in other cane begonia breeding such as 'Sophie Cecile'. Pinch young growth to encourage a fuller, bushier habit and let the topsoil dry slightly between waterings.

common_name: Ohyodogawa Sacred Lily (Japanese Omoto Breeding-Line Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant divisions in rich, well-drained soil in light to deep shade; Ohyodogawa is a Japanese Rohdea japonica collector cultivar documented chiefly as a parent of 'Goin' Curlin''.

directions: Grow in humus-rich, well-drained soil in light to deep shade, where this slow-spreading evergreen clump-former tolerates deeper shade than almost any other foliage perennial. Ohyodogawa is a Japanese Rohdea japonica (Omoto) collector cultivar, named for the Oyodo River in Miyazaki Prefecture in the naming tradition common among Japanese Rohdea selections. It is documented in Western nursery trade chiefly as one parent, crossed with 'Tancho', of the dwarf twisted-leaf cultivar 'Goin' Curlin'', brought out of Japan as an unnamed seedling by the late collector Alan Galloway; a detailed description of Ohyodogawa's own leaf form has not survived translation into English-language sources. Divide congested offsets in spring if propagation is desired, though this slow-growing species resents frequent disturbance.
sources: Plant Delights Nursery / Juniper Level Botanic Garden

common_name: Uwodu Butterfly Iris (Historic 1928 Berry White-Flowered Cultivar)

planting.note: Divide rhizomes or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade in spring; Uwodu is a vigorously spreading, white-flowered selection of the butterfly iris.

directions: Divide rhizomes or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade. Uwodu was bred by American malacologist and amateur iris hybridizer Samuel Stillman Berry and registered in 1928, producing smaller, well-rounded white flowers marked with deep violet haft spots around a yellow crest, held above pleated bright green foliage. Its stoloniferous rhizomes spread to form colonies up to three feet across, somewhat more vigorous in spread than typical clumps of the species, making it useful as a naturalizing groundcover under high tree canopy. Keep soil consistently moist through the growing season and allow the evergreen fans to remain over winter in mild climates.
